readerTitle: Three engineers, one app, and nobody in charge
caseNote: 가상 사례 (세 엔지니어의 앱 창업, 식품 유통사 내부 파일럿 팀) · 적용 레슨: 역할과 의사결정권, 베스팅
insight: 지분이 똑같은 공동창업자일수록 결정권은 영역별로 나누고, 지분은 시간이 지나며 얻도록 설계해야 한다.
misconception: 지분을 똑같이 나누면 모든 결정도 똑같이 함께 내려야 공평하고, 처음부터 지분을 다 주는 것이 서로를 믿는다는 표시다.

sources.text: 스타트업 실무의 표준 개념 (역할과 의사결정권, 창업자 지분 베스팅)
모든 인물과 상황은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 4년 베스팅과 1년 클리프는 미국 스타트업에서 흔한 구조이지만 나라와 계약마다 다릅니다. 카드에는 'a common setup'으로만 적고 법률 조언은 하지 않았습니다.
계산 확인: 33% 지분을 4년 베스팅하면 1년 클리프 시점에 그 지분의 1/4(회사 전체의 약 8%)이 베스팅됩니다. 8개월에 떠나면 클리프 전이라 베스팅된 지분은 0입니다. 미베스팅 지분이 회사로 돌아가는 방식은 계약에 따라 다르므로 'usually'로 표현했습니다.

cards.title: Three engineers, one app, and nobody in charge
body: Maya, Tom and Ravi are building a scheduling app for dental clinics. All three write code. They split the company three ways, 33% each, and shook hands on it.
It feels perfectly fair. Two quiet problems are already hiding in that handshake.

image.label: Three developers at one desk, three laptops, one empty chair labeled customers
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 세 명의 개발자가 한 책상에 나란히 앉아 각자 노트북을 보고 있고, 맞은편에 'Customers'라고 적힌 빈 의자가 하나 놓여 있음. 실제 앱 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Who decides what gets built?
body: Two weeks in, they argue for days about whether to build online booking or appointment reminders first. Nobody budges.
What rule should they set?

options.text: Decide everything together. Nothing moves until all three agree
options.feedback: It feels fair, but with three equal voices every choice becomes a negotiation. This is the trap from **roles and decision rights**: equal ownership doesn't mean every decision is shared.

options.text: Take a majority vote on every question
options.feedback: Votes break ties fast. But the outvoted founder may be the one doing the work, and repeated 2–1 votes can harden into camps.

options.text: Give each founder one area with the final say, and decide only the biggest bets together
options.feedback: This is **roles and decision rights** at work. Each type of call has one owner, so most debates end with a clear decider.

cards.title: All three want the same job.
body: When they list areas, a problem appears. All three want to own the code. Nobody wants to phone dental clinics, ask about their week, or handle a price complaint.

Splitting roles forces the question nobody wanted to ask. Maya agrees to own product and customers, even though she'd rather code. Tom owns the technical design. Ravi owns money, legal paperwork and hiring.
Without that conversation, the most important job would have belonged to no one.

cards.title: Roles and decision rights
body: A **decision right** is who has the final say on a type of choice. Others can argue, but one person decides.
The founders write it on one page: each area, its owner, and a short list of decisions that need all three. Theirs are raising money, adding a founder, large hires and selling the company.
Everything else moves at the speed of one person.

image.label: Three columns: product, tech, money, plus a shared box for big decisions
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 세 개의 세로 칸에 'Maya: Product & customers', 'Tom: Technical design', 'Ravi: Money & hiring'. 아래에 세 칸을 잇는 가로 상자 'Decide together: fundraising, new founder, big hires, selling the company'.

cards.title: How should their shares work?
body: Before signing papers, Tom says: "We trust each other. Let's just each own our 33% today." Ravi has hinted a big company keeps calling him.
What should they do?

options.text: Issue all shares now. Trust is the point
options.feedback: Simple and warm, but if anyone leaves early, they keep a third of a company they no longer build. **Vesting** exists for exactly this.

options.text: All three earn their shares over four years, with a one-year cliff
options.feedback: This is **vesting**: ownership is earned by staying. It protects whoever stays, and nobody is singled out.

options.text: Put vesting only on Ravi, since he's the likely one to leave
options.feedback: It covers the visible risk, but anyone can leave for illness, family or burnout. Singling out one founder also damages trust on day one.

cards.title: Why vesting matters more with three.
body: Suppose Ravi leaves at month eight. Without **vesting**, he keeps 33%. Maya and Tom do all the work for the rest, and future investors see a large owner who is gone.

With a common setup of four years and a one-year cliff, nothing vests before month twelve. Ravi would leave with none, and his unvested shares usually go back to the company. Had he stayed a year, a quarter of his shares, about 8% of the company, would be his.

image.label: Timeline: four years, cliff at year one, shares filling in monthly after
image.brief: 가로 타임라인 0~48개월. 12개월 지점에 'Cliff' 표시와 함께 막대가 25%까지 한 번에 차오르고, 이후 매달 조금씩 차올라 48개월에 100%. 8개월 지점에 'Ravi leaves?' 말풍선.

cards.title: Neither tool solves people problems.
body: Roles drift. Once the app has paying clinics, Maya may need to sell full time while Tom needs help with code. Review the roles page every few months.
Vesting doesn't fix a bad partner. It only limits the damage when someone leaves. A cliff can also feel harsh to someone forced out at month eleven, so agree in advance how you'd handle that.
Share agreements differ by country. Get local legal advice before signing.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a bigger company.
body: A regional food distributor asks three managers, from sales, the warehouse and finance, to pilot same-day delivery. None of them is the others' boss.
Three months in, it stalls. Sales promises delivery windows the warehouse can't meet. What fixes it?

options.text: Send every dispute up to the CEO
options.feedback: Fights get settled, but the CEO becomes the bottleneck and the team learns not to decide.

options.text: Sales owns customer promises within limits the warehouse sets; finance owns the budget; one lead breaks ties
options.feedback: **Roles and decision rights** work the same without shares. Each call has one owner, and promises stay inside what the warehouse can deliver.

options.text: Hold a weekly meeting and talk until everyone agrees
options.feedback: Talking feels collaborative, but it's the three-engineer trap again. Equal voices with no decider means the pilot moves at the pace of the slowest argument.

cards.title: Equal partners still need clear owners and earned shares.
body: This lesson used two ideas. **Roles and decision rights** gave each type of call one owner. **Vesting** made ownership something founders earn by staying.
**Try it today:** list the five decisions your team argues about most. Next to each, write one name. Where you can't, that's your next conversation.
